title: The History of Glam Rock and How It Put an End to the Hippie Era
description:

body:
in History, Music |   	August 7th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Cast your mind back to the dis­tant year 2021 and recall, if you will, its music, its fash­ions, the obses­sions of its youth. This prob­a­bly won’t be a dif­fi­cult task, since in most respects — the damp­en­ing effects of the pan­dem­ic notwith­stand­ing — none of those aspects of pop­u­lar cul­ture seem any dif­fer­ent today. Yet rough­ly the same time span sep­a­rat­ed Scott McKen­zie’s “San Fran­cis­co (Be Sure to Wear Flow­ers in Your Hair)” and David Bowie’s “Star­man.” 1967 was the year of the Sum­mer of Love; by 1972, accord­ing to most reck­on­ings, the cul­tur­al era known as the Six­ties was, if not quite over, then at least clear­ly in its final days. The hip­pies were on their way down, and glam rock­ers had arisen to take their place with a vengeance.
In less than half an hour, the new video from Band­splain­ing tells the whole sto­ry of glam rock, “the gen­der-bend­ing pro­to-punk move­ment that was hat­ed by the press and crim­i­nal­ly under­played in the U.S.” It begins in the 1970s, a time when the mar­ket for long-play­ing records was robust, but sin­gles had fall­en behind as a youth-ori­ent­ed pop-cul­tur­al form.
Into that vac­u­um stepped T. Rex, a one­time avant-garde folk duo rein­vent­ed as a straight-ahead rock band bent on reviv­ing that genre as it row­di­ly was before the Bea­t­les came along. When they hit it big, oth­er acts imi­tat­ed not just their bluesy sound, but the androg­y­nous, brazen­ly fab­ri­ca­tion-for­ward image of front­man Marc Bolan. Prac­ti­cal­ly overnight, the name of the game changed from earnest self-expres­sion to out­landish self-cre­ation.
Oth­er bands reshaped by this glam rock move­ment, as it was soon dubbed in the British media, includ­ed Slade, The Sweet, and Mott the Hoople. “My broth­er’s back at home with his Bea­t­les and his Stones,” sang that last out­fit in their break­out hit. “We nev­er got it off on that rev­o­lu­tion stuff.” That song, “All the Young Dudes,” had been writ­ten by the sin­gle most defin­ing glam-rock fig­ure: David Bowie, who him­self shot to promi­nence in the thor­ough­ly anti-Six­ties guise of Zig­gy Star­dust, the bisex­u­al, syn­thet­ics-clad rock­er from out­er space who swag­gered as if already famous across the uni­verse. With­in a few years, Bowie’s anten­na for the zeit­geist would have him retir­ing Zig­gy Star­dust and ditch­ing glam rock, a genre whose flame burned as bril­liant­ly — and indeed gar­ish­ly — as it did briefly. But in pop music, its char­ac­ter­is­tic lack of sociopo­lit­i­cal ideals, obses­sion with fame, and casu­al rela­tion­ship with real­i­ty were here to stay.

title: How Ancient Greek Warships Worked: The Engineering of the Trireme Explained in 3D Animation
description:

body:
in History, Technology |   	August 6th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Recall, if you will, the first time you read Book 2 of Home­r’s Ili­ad. The sec­tion like­ly to have giv­en you the most trou­ble — unless, of course, you’re blessed with an obses­sive inter­est in ancient naval war­fare — is the much-remarked-upon Cat­a­logue of Ships, a run­down of not just the con­tin­gents of the Achaean army sail­ing to Troy, but also the ships they’re doing it in. How­ev­er evoca­tive Home­r’s poet­ry, more than a few mod­ern read­ers may face a cer­tain dif­fi­cul­ty imag­in­ing ancient Greek ves­sels for them­selves. For­tu­nate­ly for them, the YouTube chan­nel Decon­struct­ed recent­ly put out the video above, which uses 3D imagery to explain the work­ings of an entire trireme, part by his­tor­i­cal­ly accu­rate part.
And what is a trireme? Two and a half mil­len­nia ago, says the video’s nar­ra­tor, it was “the most pow­er­ful war­ship in the Mediter­ranean.” This despite the fact that it had “no engine, no can­nons, and no heavy armor”: just “a nar­row wood­en hull, a bronze ram, and 170 men row­ing in per­fect rhythm.”
Wel­come to ancient Greece, where raw, syn­chro­nized man­pow­er could win a major war. Named for the “three super­im­posed tiers of one-man oars on each side of the ves­sel,” the trireme “pushed the tech­no­log­i­cal lim­its of the ancient world, with every part of its design opti­mized for speed and maneu­ver­abil­i­ty.” So swift was its accel­er­a­tion, regard­less of wind con­di­tions, that a sin­gle strike of its bronze ram could prove deci­sive.
Among the most effec­tive maneu­vers for a fleet of triremes were the diek­plous, in which the ships “rode through gaps in the ene­my for­ma­tion, then turned to attack the exposed sterns of oppos­ing ships,” and the periplous, in which they sailed “around the ene­my line to attack from the side or rear.” Not that Homer had rea­son to sing of such tac­tics, at least as per­formed by triremes, which were only put into use in the sev­enth cen­tu­ry BC. That was five or six hun­dred years after the notion­al peri­od of the leg­endary Tro­jan War, which, as the Ili­ad tells us, involved tri­a­con­ters and pen­te­con­ters, ships pro­pelled by a mere 30 to 50 oars­men as against the 170 stacked into the trireme. Even in those days, as Home­r’s con­tem­po­rary lis­ten­ers would have felt, tech­nol­o­gy was march­ing on — with the tech­nol­o­gy of war at the fore­front.

title: Under Glass Cloches, Amber Cowan Nests Enchanting Flameworked Scenes
description: Known for her lush assemblages of flameworked glass, Amber Cowan reimagines a ubiquitous yet fragile medium. Flowers, filigree, and colorful baubl
body:
Known for her lush assemblages of flameworked glass, Amber Cowan reimagines a ubiquitous yet fragile medium. Flowers, filigree, and colorful baubles cluster into dense compositions that invoke fairytale narratives and whimsical nature scenes. Cowan typically works with industrial scraps, antiques, and other offcasts, which allows her to draw on products and colorways that are no longer in production.
Currently leaning into cloche and coupe sculptures alongside her wall-based works, the Philadelphia-based artist is preparing for several upcoming exhibitions, including at San Francisco’s Museum of Craft and Design in September and Design Miami in December. Her work is on view now in The Passion of Collecting at The Baker Museum in Naples, Florida, and you can find more on Instagram.

title: A Short Film Sheds Light on the Garfield Phones Washing Up on a French Beach Since the '80s
description: Amid the rugged, wave-churned shoreline of France’s Breton coast, a surprising tidbit of pop culture has kept beachcombers returning for more than
body:
Amid the rugged, wave-churned shoreline of France’s Breton coast, a surprising tidbit of pop culture has kept beachcombers returning for more than 40 years. The short film “Silly Little Plastic Cat” transports us to this slice of Brittany, where local residents grew up collecting parts of a 1984 Garfield-themed plastic telephone on the beach—and still do. Photographer and director Zack Grant, founder the production studio 2020 Land, was intrigued by the story, which made news a few years back after the source of the dispersed merchandise was finally discovered.
The part of Brittany where the phones wash up is situated along a busy shipping thoroughfare. At some point during their transit in the mid-1980s, the shipping container carrying thousands of the units fell into the sea, and over the years, its spilled contents have continued to arrive in distinctively orange, tangled jumbles. As quirky as it is, the phenomenon also shines a light on the less humorous side: the vast quantity of garbage that washes ashore.



To put the scale of pollution into perspective, nearly 1,500 shipping containers were lost in 2025 alone. Less than 10 percent of those were recovered; the rest are still missing. It’s a small fraction of the hundreds of millions of containers transported annually, yet a single 40-foot container could hold the contents of an entire three- or four-bedroom house or around 400 mattresses. Multiply that by several hundred and consider everything we ship—clothing, medical supplies, car parts, you name it—and we can start to scratch the surface of the oceans’ staggering garbage patches.
“Silly Little Plastic Cat” illuminates the reality of pollution and also highlights how locals are motivated to help. Residents have adopted Garfield as something of a de facto mascot for cleanup projects. “We are 100 percent responsible for the current climate situation and current pollution,” says a local conservationist who aids in beach cleanups via Surfrider Foundation. “We are also actors in the solutions.” Another initiative invites people to work together to regenerate older or damaged items, making them usable once again while reducing consumption.
See more on Grant’s work on Vimeo.

title: New York City's Last Standing Wood Column Company Closes After 110 Years
description: 110 years ago, Thomas Lupo’s grandfather opened the American Wood Column Corporation in Brooklyn’s Williamsburg neighborhood. Specializing in arch
body:
110 years ago, Thomas Lupo’s grandfather opened the American Wood Column Corporation in Brooklyn’s Williamsburg neighborhood. Specializing in architectural woodwork including decorative moulding, columns, balusters, corbels, and more, the historic family-owned company is shutting down after more than a century. A new documentary directed and produced by filmmaker and photographer Joshua Charrow takes viewers on one final walk-through of the factory.
A vast collection of about 6,000 handmade wooden molds—many of them reverse carved molds—cover the walls and correspond to numbered samples for reference. “My grandfather bought these molds used, and they were used,” Lupo explains. “So they’ve got to be over 200 years old.”



Throughout the film, Charrow follows Lupo around the building, documenting the owner’s favorite pieces and timeless anecdotes. Among these works are six-foot pencils, ornamental department store columns, set designs from Saturday Night Live, grave details from The Godfather, The Exorcist stairway, and more.
Filled with family stories and nostalgic memories of growing up inside a woodworking studio, Lupo is cognizant of the fact that he, too, is growing older. His team, who has been with him for close to 40 years, believe it’s also time to retire gracefully. “I will be closing down the business. It’s not a question of if, it’s a question of when. That’s all.” he says. “Like anything else, everything changes. Time goes on.”
Watch the full video on YouTube.

title: The Winners of the 2026 Pure Street Photography Awards Invoke Happenstance and Commotion
description: From happenstance and humor to solemnity and tension, the images topping the 2026 Pure Street Photography Awards run the gamut of daily scenes. Th
body:
From happenstance and humor to solemnity and tension, the images topping the 2026 Pure Street Photography Awards run the gamut of daily scenes. The annual contest is organized into two categories: black-and-white and open. Reflections of New York City meet dramatic views of urban spaces and pensive tableaux in rural communities, emphasizing timely and candid moments that center diverse human experiences.
This year, eight winners were selected from nearly 1,600 entries submitted by photographers in 50 countries. An exhibition of 158 of the top images is slated to pop up at Jawahar Kala Kendra in Jaipur, India, from November 20 to 22. The open call is also now live for the 2027 edition, and you can see more and follow updates on the competition’s Instagram.

title: A Menagerie of Animal Sculptures by 50+ Artists Populate 'The Ark'
description: The term “ark” invariably conjures images of the monumental boat onto which pairs of animals were stewarded prior to a cataclysmic, biblical flood
body:
The term “ark” invariably conjures images of the monumental boat onto which pairs of animals were stewarded prior to a cataclysmic, biblical flood. It’s a reference that feels apt amid the climate crisis and our planet’s rising sea levels, although in this case, the melting ice caps and creeping tides are down to us. The large-scale exhibition titled The Ark at Powerhouse Arts asks, will we care for the future of our planet the way we care for the animals we love?
The presentation draws directly on the myth if The Deluge from Genesis, “an event of epic scale that becomes a metaphor for the present moment, where environmental and social upheaval converge,” says a statement. “Throughout the exhibition—experienced in the round, in close proximity, and at monumental scale—the animals function as both protagonists and interlocutors.”
Installation view of ‘The Ark’ at Powerhouse Arts, Summer 2026. Photo by Xavier Petromelis
Colossal readers may recognize the work of Kiki Smith, Nichola Theakston, Anthony Theakston, Wangechi Mutu, Jeffrey Gibson, and more. In all, more than 50 artists are represented through 90 sculptures and installations. The pieces run the gamut of materials, from wood and stone carvings to cast bronze and resin. A group of pigeons by Maurizio Cattelan perch on structural beams and both Nichola and Anthony Theakstons’ bronzes speak to the sacredness of animals, while John O’Reilly’s rendition of an emaciated female dog crouching over her pup plucks a heart-rending chord. Throughout the exhibition, emotional evocations span joy, amazement, humor, trepidation, and grief.
Curated by artist Eric Fischl, the show was first staged at The Church in Sag Harbor, a historical whaling town. Now in Brooklyn, the The Ark lands in the former warehouse space of Powerhouse Arts, a nonprofit dedicated to fabrication and production, on the Gowanus Canal. The building is known as the “Batcave” and sits adjacent to what’s designated by the Environmental Protection Agency as a Superfund site, a heavily polluted area in need of concerted cleanup efforts.
The physical location and its surroundings present a post-industrial background to a show about nature, the environment, and material exploration. Visitors are invited to walk through a room filled with animals from floor to ceiling, invoking elements of surprise and wonder. Powerhouse Arts adds, “Rather than framing environmental themes through notions of crisis and urgency alone, the exhibition centers on relationships and intimate encounters.”
The Ark continues through August 30 in Brooklyn. Find more on the organization’s Instagram.
